items.title: Section: Why the First Absorption Still Carries a Trace of Suffering

items.zh: 問：何緣故，知初靜慮中苦根未斷？答：彼品麁重未遠離故。若於是處苦根已斷，便與第二靜慮住時應無差別。是故當知是處未斷。
items.en: Question: how is it known that the root of suffering remains uncut in the first absorption? Answer: because the coarse heaviness of that class has not yet been left behind. If suffering were already cut here, there would be no difference from abiding in the second absorption. Therefore one should know it is not yet cut here.

items.title: Section: Why Called Agitated, Relative Not Absolute

items.zh: 問：若尋伺等於初靜慮等中皆能攝益勝三摩地，又能攝受自地靜慮皆令清淨，何因緣故，世尊於彼顯示動名？答：此望他地，不望自地。問：何因緣故，從欲界上於初靜慮等中，建立後後勝上支分？答：當知略有三因緣故。一、所治能治故；二、證得勝利故；三、所證得故。
items.en: Question: if investigation, reflection, and the rest benefit and purify their own stage of absorption, why does the Buddha describe these absorptions using the language of agitation? Answer: this is relative to a higher stage, not to the stage itself. Answer: there are, briefly, three causes — the relationship of what is overcome to what overcomes it, the benefit attained, and what is actually realised.

items.zh: 當知如是三種因緣，四靜慮中五支所攝，隨其所應。

items.title: Section: Three Pairwise Differences Complete the Four Absorptions

items.zh: 問：初二靜慮有何差別？答：第二靜慮中三摩地圓滿有差別故。問：第二、第三靜慮、有何差別？答：第三靜慮饒益圓滿有差別故。問：第三、第四靜慮有何差別？答：第四靜慮清淨圓滿、有差別故。
items.en: Question: what is the difference between the first and second absorptions? Answer: the second absorption has the difference of complete concentration. Question: what is the difference between the second and third? Answer: the third has the difference of complete benefit. Question: what is the difference between the third and fourth? Answer: the fourth has the difference of complete purity.

items.title: Section: A Third Topic Opens — Four Ways of Cultivating Concentration

items.zh: 復有四種修三摩地。一者、為得現法樂住故；二者、為得勝智見故；三者、為得分別慧故；四者、為證諸漏永盡故。當知依四補特伽羅，建立四種修三摩地。云何四種補特伽羅？謂苦速通，已得行迹、已見諦者。
items.en: There are also four ways of cultivating concentration: to dwell in present-life bliss; to attain superior knowledge and vision; to attain discerning wisdom; and to realise the complete exhaustion of outflows. One should know that four kinds of person correspond to these four ways of cultivating concentration. What are the four kinds of person? Painful-swift, one who has not yet attained the course of root absorption but has already seen the truths.

items.title: Section: Four Kinds of Person Matched to Four Ways of Practising

items.zh: 復有異生，未得行迹、已得有情所緣無量、已離欲者。又樂遲通，已得行迹、已見諦者。又樂速通，已得行迹、已見諦者。此中異生，已得無量、已離欲者，若已證得死生智通，當知是名智見清淨。若樂遲通行迹轉時，雖已見諦，由軟根故而名退法。由此因緣，復於欲界受想尋思，當住正念、當起正知。
items.en: There is also an ordinary being who has not yet attained the course of root absorption, yet has attained the immeasurable focused on beings, and has become free of desire. There is also pleasant-slow, one who has attained the course of root absorption and has already seen the truths. There is also pleasant-swift, one who has attained the course of root absorption and has already seen the truths. When one of pleasant-slow progress is turning along this course, though the truths have already been seen, due to soft faculties this is called subject to falling back. Because of this, one should maintain mindfulness and give rise to clear knowing towards feeling, perception, and deliberation in the desire realm.

items.zh: 復次，諸靜慮離欲所顯。當知離欲略有六種。一、自性離欲，二、損減離欲，三、任持離欲，四、昇進離欲，五、愚癡離欲，六、對治離欲。

items.title: Section: Six Kinds of Freedom from Desire, Only One of Which Actually Cuts It

items.zh: 自性離欲者，謂於自性不淨非所受用事中諸厭背性；又於苦受諸厭背性；又若已離初靜慮染住，於第二靜慮等中，於尋伺等諸厭背性。是名自性離欲。損減離欲者，謂兩兩交會習婬欲法，除熱惱已諸厭背性。如是等類所餘應知，皆名損減離欲。任持離欲者，謂諸有受用美妙飲食極飽滿已，於餘飲食諸厭背性。如是等類所餘應知，皆名任持離欲。昇進離欲者，謂已獲得勝上財寶，或尊貴位，於餘下劣諸厭背性。如是等類所餘應知，皆名昇進離欲。愚癡離欲者，謂於涅槃甚深功德不能解了，遂於涅槃生厭背性。如是等類所餘應知，皆名愚癡離欲。對治離欲者，謂由厭壞對治故，或由斷對治故，或由持對治故，或由遠分對治故，或由世間出世間道斷諸煩惱，如是皆名對治離欲。
items.en: Freedom through its own nature is aversion arising towards what is inherently impure and unfit for enjoyment; towards painful feeling; and, once absorption is left behind for a higher stage, towards investigation, reflection, and the rest. This is called freedom through its own nature. Freedom through antidote is through the antidote of disgust, the antidote that severs, the antidote that sustains, the antidote of further distancing, or through severing affliction by a worldly or transcendent path; all of these are called freedom through antidote.

items.title: Section: Four Names for the Same Settled Mind, and Ten Ways It Can Be Lost

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，說諸靜慮名為住耶？答：繫心於內所緣境界，於外所緣不流散故。問：何因緣故，說諸靜慮名三摩地？答：於所知事同分所緣一切影像，平等平等[＊]住持心故。問：何因緣故，說諸靜慮名奢摩他？答：為欲寂靜一切煩惱正安止故。問：何因緣故，說諸靜慮名心一境性？答：略有二種所緣境界。一、不定地所緣境界，二者、定地所緣境界。此中一境，所謂定地所緣境界，非第二境。繫心於此一所緣境，是故說名心一境性。復次，當知此中，從離欲退，略有十種。謂或依止不平等故，從離欲退。
items.en: Question: why are the absorptions called abiding? Answer: because the mind is bound to an internal object and does not scatter towards external objects. Question: why are they called samādhi? Answer: because the mental image corresponding to the object known matches it evenly, sustaining the mind. Question: why are they called calm-abiding? Answer: in order to still every affliction and settle correctly. There are also, briefly, ten kinds of falling back from freedom from desire. The first is falling back due to the elements falling out of balance.

blocks.text: Why the Buddha called the first three meditations "agitated", and the four kinds of practitioner: painful or pleasant, slow or swift.
Master Cháng Bǎi: unpliancy and instability are not entirely gone in the first meditation.
Master Cháng Bǎi: the first meditation's thinking is agitation relative to the second, not relative to itself. The Buddha called the first three "agitated" with a hidden intent.
Master Cháng Bǎi: the second is complete in concentration; the third complete in benefit, with body and mind in bliss.

Master Cháng Bǎi: painful means lacking root absorption; swift means sharp faculties. Of the four persons, one with soft faculties should abide in mindfulness and arouse clear knowing towards feeling, perception, and thought.

subs.head: Six kinds of freedom from desire

blocks.text: Master Cháng Bǎi: by the worldly path afflictions are subdued; by the transcendent path, cut. (Untranslated, 0650a16: the six kinds: by nature, by weakening, by support, by advance, by delusion, and by antidote.)

subs.head: Four names; ten ways to lose it

blocks.text: Every absorption binds the mind to an inner object. Calm abiding means stopping, keeping the mind on one object. When the body's elements are in conflict and grave illness arises, one cannot enter concentration and falls back.
Some practitioners progress painfully and slowly. The treatise lists them without blame; there is a method for each.

quiz.q: How is it known that the root of suffering remains uncut in the first absorption?
options: grief is still present there and grief is the root of pain, nothing to do with heaviness, the clearest proof
breathing is still present there
its class's coarse heaviness is not yet left behind; if cut, it would not differ from the second
there is no pleasant feeling there
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: unpliancy and instability are not yet entirely gone, and they still obstruct entering concentration. So the root of pain is known by its coarse heaviness, and the argument is that otherwise the first two absorptions would not differ.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain that there would be no difference from the second absorption?
options: both have investigation, so methods would be the same, and it would need no treatment at all
their lifespans would be the same
both have joy and pleasure, so abiding in the factors of benefit they would not differ
their birthplaces would be the same
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the first has joy and pleasure, and so does the second; abiding in the factors of benefit, they would hardly differ. Investigation is not shared by them, so the argument rests on the feelings.

quiz.q: This is rendered "why does the Buddha describe them using the language of agitation." What is wrong with "them"?
options: per the lecture 彼 is the absorptions, while "them" follows investigation and reads as that
none: 彼 is investigation alone, the absorptions never being called agitated, as the lecture has it
世尊 should be "the sage"
動 should be "restlessness"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the Blessed One gave the name of agitation to the first three absorptions, with a hidden intent. So 彼 refers to the absorptions; the English places "them" right after investigation and reflection.

quiz.q: How does the treatise differentiate the four absorptions?
options: the second complete purity, the third concentration, the fourth benefit, having the most
the second has complete concentration, the third complete benefit, and the fourth complete purity
the second benefit, the third purity, the fourth concentration
all three complete purity
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the second is complete in concentration, while the first is not, as investigation still stirs. The third is complete in benefit, and the fourth in purity. Each difference names what that stage brings to completion.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain the third's complete benefit, and the fourth's purity?
options: the third's heaven has the most wealth, and the fourth keeps precepts best
the third has investigation, the fourth joy
in the third feeling is fullest, with bliss and no stirring joy; the fourth is free from all four feelings' disturbance
the third lacks bliss, the fourth has it
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: in the third the benefit factor of feeling is most complete, with body and mind in bliss and no stirring of joy. The fourth is neutral feeling, free of the disturbance of pain, pleasure, grief, and joy, and so very pure.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain superior knowledge and vision?
options: non-conceptual wisdom directly seeing suchness, for sages only, with no link to the divine eye, always
wisdom from hearing the Dharma
the view that precepts are pure
practice preparing for the divine eye; being able to illumine and see objects of form is called vision
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: a practitioner cultivates concentration as the preparatory path towards the divine eye; illuminating and observing objects of form is called vision. The goal is thus a supernormal knowing, not the wisdom of seeing the truths.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi define painful, pleasant, slow, and swift?
options: painful means illness and pleasant health, slow a late ordination and swift an early one in the order
painful has affliction, pleasant none; slow and swift concern lifespan
painful lacks root absorption, pleasant has it; slow has dull faculties, swift has sharp ones
painful is poverty, pleasant wealth; slow and swift concern age
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: painful means lacking root concentration, so body and mind do not experience pleasure; pleasant means having it. Slow means faith and the other faculties are dull, and swift that they are sharp. Two criteria thus combine.

quiz.q: Why does the treatise call one of pleasant-slow progress subject to falling back?
options: due to soft faculties
because lacking root absorption, none of the merits are firm
because the person keeps no precepts
because the person does not hear the Dharma
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the third person, of pleasant-slow progress, has root absorption, dull faculties, and realisation of the truths. The treatise gives soft faculties as the reason, so lacking absorption cannot be it, as this person has absorption.

quiz.q: What aversions does the treatise cite under freedom through its own nature?
options: towards all wholesome dharmas, pleasant feeling, and the Jewels, since desire-free ones turn from all
towards sexual objects alone
towards wealth alone
towards what is inherently impure and unfit, towards painful feeling, and towards investigation once left behind
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: one feels aversion towards desires that are impure by nature and not fit for enjoyment. The treatise adds painful feeling and, in the higher absorptions, investigation and the rest. The English lacks the heading that lists six kinds, so the total is not tested.

quiz.q: This is rendered "once absorption is left behind for a higher stage." What is lost?
options: 染: what is left is the stain of the first absorption, not absorption itself
nothing: one abandons absorption when moving up, as the lecture says at each step
苦受 is lost
厭背 is lost
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: taking the second as an example, the third turns from the joy of the second, and the fourth from the bliss of the third. One remains in absorption while turning from lower factors, so what is left is a stain, not absorption.

quiz.q: Does Master Cháng Bǎi say that freedom from desire requires cutting afflictions?
options: not necessarily; simply not delighting in one's own objects is called freedom from desire
it does: only cutting all desire-realm seeds counts, and the rest are mere names
only arhats count as free of desire
only rebirth in the form realm counts
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the kinds of freedom from desire simply mean not delighting in each one's object, and do not necessarily require severing. Note that he speaks of the full list of six, of which the English has kept only two.

quiz.q: Why does the treatise call the absorptions calm-abiding?
options: because the image matches its object evenly, sustaining the mind
because the mind is bound inward and does not scatter
because it draws forth powers
in order to still every affliction and settle correctly
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: calm-abiding means stopping, keeping the mind on one kind of object without changing it. Option B answers why they are called samādhi, and C why they are called abiding, so three close answers must be told apart.
